A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UIKA. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and reenactment results, quantitative ablations in Tables 2–4, and additional qualitative experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds latency measurements, dataset-consistency results, and human ratings in Tables S2–S4.

M1.justification: The reported facial-correspondence estimator changes substantially: v1 uses a frozen VGGT backbone, including DINOv2 and frozen attention; v3 uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 followed by four trainable alternating frame/global-attention stages. Appendix A.1 and the architecture diagrams establish changed components and trainability. The downstream UV/screen attention, fusion, losses, and animation procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds CAP4D-generated head sequences to a spatial and temporal dataset-quality evaluation in Table S3. The reconstruction training datasets, VFHQ/NeRSemble-v2 evaluations, reenactment tasks, and previously demonstrated stylized and in-the-wild domains remain unchanged.

E2.justification: CAP4D-generated data becomes an evaluated comparator in Table S3, whereas v1 only discusses CAP4D as related work. The main reconstruction baseline sets remain unchanged, and the user study reuses those methods. The two FastAvatar additions to Table 1 are capability comparisons, without reported reconstruction evaluations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces three additional evaluation protocols: timing with 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 inputs; spatial and temporal warping-error assessment; and human ratings from 1–5 for rendering quality, motion consistency, and identity preservation. Existing benchmark splits, reconstruction metrics, and stated training budgets are retained. The PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds view-count sensitivity analysis for inference latency and quantitative analysis of synthetic-data spatial/temporal consistency. New Figure S4 also supplies additional with/without-synthetic-data examples testing 3D consistency. The earlier training-data, UV-attention, aggregation, and fixed-fusion-weight ablations remain present.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its experiments. The new latency, consistency, and human-rating tables report point values without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain identical numerical results. New Tables S2–S4 report latency increasing from 1.96 seconds for one input to 32.9 seconds for 32 inputs, lower synthetic-data warping errors than CAP4D-generated data, and UIKA user scores of 4.37, 4.17, and 4.23 for rendering, motion, and identity respectively. These substantially broaden reported findings without establishing a same-setting reconstruction improvement.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly states an O(N^2) dependence of view-dependent processing on input count, attributed to self-attention. This is a limited analytical scaling claim without a derivation. The main mathematical definitions and Equations (1)–(15) remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: arbitrary pose-free inputs, UV-guided correspondence and attention, adaptive appearance fusion, synthetic training data, and strong monocular/multi-view reconstruction. Replacing 'unposed' with 'pose-free' does not change their scope.

C2.justification: v3 explains how the revised attention stages capture within-frame structure and across-frame correspondence. Its latency discussion also distinguishes view-dependent avatar construction from view-independent animation, clarifying computational bottlenecks. The existing FLAME expressiveness, demographic-bias, and many-view scalability limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 specifies the revised estimator's ViT-B/16 backbone, four attention stages, and trainability, while removing the former 518×518 resizing instructions. Appendix A.4 adds a 3 ms LBS and 2 ms rendering breakdown. Table S1, main training resources, and the disclosed project-page address remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises research positioning through new discussion of diffusion-transformer and audio-driven approaches, MVP4D, and recent Gaussian-avatar methods including Fast-GHA, FlexAvatar, and two distinct FastAvatar papers. Several earlier citations are removed. Pixel3DMM remains the same cited work despite updated publication information.

P1.justification: All three Related Work subsections are substantially rewritten, and Appendix A.1 receives a replacement architectural explanation. The supplementary roadmap and subsection organization are revised, terminology is standardized to 'pose-free,' and acknowledgments are added. Most other method and main-experiment prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables S2–S4 and Figure S4, redraws the estimator architecture from v1 Figure S3 as Figure S2, and reorganizes early appendix figures and Table S1. Table 1 gains two FastAvatar rows, and captions are restyled. Most main qualitative displays and later appendix galleries are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's limited timing disclosure and largely qualitative support for synthetic-data consistency, v3 provides useful measurements in Tables S2–S3 and clearer architectural documentation. Human ratings add another assessment perspective. The gains are limited by missing participant/stimulus counts and uncertainty reporting, and by the absence of evidence connecting the revised estimator to the unchanged main benchmark results. Overall, the added support and transparency provide a modest quality improvement.
